subject: system-design
title: Design Uber
summary: Match a rider with a nearby driver in real time. It is a geospatial problem that has to absorb a flood of driver location updates while answering fast 'who's near me' queries.

blocks.text: Uber's core job is matching: a rider requests a trip and the system must find a suitable driver near them, fast. Underneath it's a geospatial problem with an awkward shape. Drivers report their location constantly (a heavy write stream) while riders ask for nearby drivers (a latency-sensitive read). The design lives or dies on indexing locations to serve both.

items: Functional: request a ride, find nearby available drivers, match, and track the trip live.
Real-time location: drivers push location every few seconds; riders see the car move.
Pricing including surge, and payment captured after the trip ends.
Low-latency matching; correctness under churn as drivers go on- and off-line.

blocks.text: Millions of active drivers, each sending a location update every few seconds. That's millions of writes per second, the dominant load. Nearby-search queries are fewer but must return in milliseconds. Trips themselves are comparatively rare events, so the system is shaped by the location firehose, not the ride count.

Driver location updates flow into a location service that maintains a geospatial index of where every available driver is right now. When a rider requests a ride, a dispatch service queries that index for nearby drivers, ranks them, and offers the trip. A separate trip service tracks the ride to completion and hands off to pricing and payments.

items: Location service ingests driver updates and maintains the live geospatial index.
Dispatch/matching service runs nearby-search and assigns a driver to a request.
Trip service tracks an in-progress ride and streams the driver's position to the rider.
Pricing service computes fares and surge multipliers from supply and demand.
Payment service charges the rider after the trip completes.

blocks.text: Raw latitude/longitude is hard to query for 'within this radius', so map the world onto a spatial index. A geohash encodes a location into a short string whose prefix length is a precision level, turning 'nearby' into a prefix match; a QuadTree recursively splits space into cells, so a search visits only the cells overlapping the query area. Either way, finding nearby drivers becomes a bounded lookup instead of a full scan.

blocks.title: Write-heavy updates vs read-heavy search
blocks.text: The location stream is overwhelmingly writes (every driver, every few seconds), while matching is reads. The same index must absorb constant updates and answer nearby-search fast, so keep the hot index in memory, often partitioned by region, and let each shard handle only its area's writes and queries. Don't index on a disk-bound store that can't take the write rate.

ETA comes from a routing/maps service using the road network, not straight-line distance. Surge pricing is computed per region from the live supply-demand ratio in the location index, raising prices where drivers are scarce. Payment is captured after the trip because the fare may depend on the actual route and time taken, so it can't be finalized up front.

blocks.title: Partition by geography
blocks.text: Sharding the location index by region keeps each shard's write and read load local and bounded, and a rider's matches almost always live in their own or an adjacent region. Geography is the natural partition key for this whole system.
